e.etymology: Anglicized from the Gaelic name Donnchadh, from donn (brown) and cath (battle). Two medieval kings of Scotland bore it, including the Duncan murdered in Shakespeare's Macbeth.
namesakes: King Duncan (Scottish king murdered in Shakespeare's Macbeth)
Duncan MacLeod (hero of the Highlander TV series)

assoc.t: Duncan Hines baking mixes
Duncan yo-yos

e.note: Sounds the same as Dunkin', the coffee and donut chain, so expect donut jokes.

e.etymology: A spelling of Natalia used mainly in Brazil and Latin America. Natalia is a Late Latin saint's name from natalis dies, the birthday of Christ, that is Christmas.
A modern American spelling of Case, also used as a clipped form of Kacey or Casey. It rose in the 2010s alongside Jace and Chase.

e.meaning: from Marlow, a place named for a lake
e.etymology: From an English surname for someone from Marlow in Buckinghamshire, a place name built on Old English mere (lake, pool). Marlowe is the more common spelling; both rose for girls in the 2010s.
namesakes: Marlow (narrator of Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness)

e.etymology: The Spanish word rubi (ruby) used as a name; like English ruby it goes back to Latin rubeus (red). In the US it is used mostly in Hispanic families and peaked after the 2004 telenovela Rubi.

assoc.t: Rubi, title character of the 2004 Mexican telenovela

e.meaning: of the Julius family; traditionally read as youthful
e.etymology: A spelling of Gillian, the medieval English form of Juliana, which is the feminine of the Roman family name Julius. Jill began as its short form.
namesakes: Jillian Michaels (fitness trainer from The Biggest Loser)

e.etymology: The Spanish and Portuguese feminine of Miguel (Michael), from Hebrew Mikha'el, the rhetorical question who is like God? English Michaela began as an anglicized form of this name.

Usually treated as a variant of Jelani, a name African American families have used since the 1970s and that is commonly described as Swahili for mighty. Today it is given mostly to girls, alongside Kalani and Leilani.

From Greek Salome, a form of a Hebrew name from the same root as shalom (peace). In the Gospels one Salome witnesses the resurrection; tradition gives the same name to the girl who asked for John the Baptist's head.
namesakes: Salome (biblical dancer; subject of Oscar Wilde's play and Richard Strauss's opera)
e.note: Best known for the story of the dancer who asked for the head of John the Baptist.

assoc.t: Salome, who asked for John the Baptist's head

e.meaning: prophet in Hebrew; also short for Indian names meaning new
e.etymology: A short name with more than one source. Hebrew navi means prophet, and in Punjabi and Hindi families Navi is a pet form of names that begin with Nav- (new), such as Navneet and Navdeep.

assoc.t: Navi, Link's fairy guide in Zelda: Ocarina of Time
the Na'vi, blue-skinned people of the Avatar films

e.etymology: The English word for a small sheltered inlet, from Old English cofa (chamber, cave). It joined the wave of nature-word names in the 2010s and 2020s.

A spelling of Kaylee, a late 20th-century name built from Kay and Lee or taken from the surname Cayley. The whole family of spellings took off after the rock band Marillion released the song Kayleigh in 1985.
A respelling of Talia with the -iyah ending made familiar by Aaliyah. Talia is the Hebrew name Talya, from tal (dew) and Yah (God), and is also a short form of Natalia.

assoc.t: Taliyah, a champion in the game League of Legends

e.etymology: From Swahili jabari (brave one), a word borrowed from Arabic jabbar (mighty, ruler). African American parents adopted it in the late 20th century.
namesakes: Jabari Parker (former NBA forward, No. 2 draft pick in 2014)
Jabari Smith Jr. (NBA forward)

assoc.t: the Jabari, M'Baku's mountain tribe in Black Panther

e.etymology: A pet form of Elizabeth, from Hebrew Elisheva, my God is an oath. It became a name in its own right and was the second most popular girls' name in America around 1930.
namesakes: Betty White (The Golden Girls actress)
Betty Ford (first lady and clinic founder)
Betty Friedan (author of The Feminine Mystique)

assoc.t: Betty Crocker, General Mills baking brand
Betty Boop, 1930s cartoon flapper
Betty Cooper of Archie comics and Riverdale
Betty Rubble of The Flintstones
betty, old surf and skate slang for an attractive girl

e.etymology: From an English surname that began as a short form of Germanic names with the element ger (spear), such as Gerard and Gerald. Actor Gary Cooper, whose stage name came from Gary, Indiana, made it a 20th-century favorite.
namesakes: Gary Cooper (classic Hollywood actor)
Gary Oldman (Oscar-winning actor)
Gary Sinise (actor, Forrest Gump)

assoc.t: Gary, Indiana, steel city near Chicago
Gary, SpongeBob SquarePants's pet snail

e.meaning: from the surname meaning son of Brian
e.etymology: A surname derived from Brian, an Irish name that probably goes back to a Celtic root meaning high or noble. It has been used as a first name in the US since the 19th century.
namesakes: Bryant Gumbel (TV journalist and sportscaster)

assoc.t: Kobe Bryant, Lakers basketball legend
Bryant Park in Midtown Manhattan
Bryant heating and cooling systems

e.etymology: A short form of Victoria, the Latin word for victory and the name of the Roman goddess of victory. Tori is also an unrelated Japanese name and the Japanese word for bird.
namesakes: Tori Amos (singer-songwriter)
Tori Spelling (Beverly Hills, 90210 actress)
Tori Kelly (singer)

e.etymology: From Sanskrit vira (hero, brave man), a distant relative of Latin vir (man). Veer is the usual English spelling of the Hindi and Punjabi form.
e.note: Spelled the same as the English verb veer, to swerve suddenly.

e.etymology: From a Scottish and English surname that comes from Old French l'isle (the island), given to someone who lived on or came from an island.
namesakes: Lyle Lovett (country singer-songwriter)
Lyle the Crocodile (children's book and film character)
Lyle Menendez (convicted with his brother Erik of killing their parents)

assoc.t: Lyle the Crocodile of the picture books and 2022 film
Lyle Menendez, convicted of killing his parents in 1989
Lyle Lovett, country singer-songwriter

e.etymology: Feminine of Erik, from Old Norse Eirikr, whose first part is read as ever or sole and whose second is rikr (ruler). Erika is the Scandinavian and German spelling of Erica.
namesakes: Erika Jayne (singer and Real Housewives of Beverly Hills star)
Erika Christensen (actress, Parenthood)

e.etymology: A recent coinage that adds the -son ending of Jackson and Grayson to Jett, or respells Jetson. Jett itself comes from jet, the black gemstone and the aircraft.

assoc.t: The Jetsons, the 1960s space-age cartoon family

e.etymology: A phonetic spelling of Casey, from the Irish surname O Cathasaigh, descendant of the watchful one. It also spells out the initials K.C.
The Turkish form of the Arabic name Uthman, borne by the third caliph of Islam. Osman I founded the Ottoman Empire around 1300, and the word Ottoman comes from his name.
namesakes: Osman I (founder of the Ottoman Empire)

e.etymology: Of unknown origin; one guess makes it a French pet form of Marc. The fame of actor Marlon Brando, who was named for his father, carried it around the English- and Spanish-speaking world.
namesakes: Marlon Brando (actor, The Godfather)
Marlon Wayans (comedian and actor)
Marlon Jackson (member of the Jackson 5)

assoc.t: Marlon Brando, star of The Godfather

e.etymology: A modern American coinage that pairs the Bray- of Brayden with the -lee ending of Kaylee and Jaylee.

e.meaning: tender, delicate (Arabic); also a Finnish form of Helena or Magdalena
e.etymology: A spelling shared by several traditions: Arabic Lina, read as tender or as a young palm tree; the Finnish short form of Helena and Magdaleena; and a girls' name used in India.
A form of Delilah, from Hebrew Delila, tied to a root meaning to weaken. Dalila is the usual spelling in Spanish, French and Arabic. In the Bible Delilah betrays Samson by having his hair cut.
namesakes: Dalilah Muhammad (Olympic champion in the 400-meter hurdles)

e.etymology: A short form of old Germanic names built on id (work, labor). It was revived in the 19th century, when it was also linked to Mount Ida of Greek mythology.
namesakes: Ida B. Wells (journalist and anti-lynching crusader)
Ida Tarbell (muckraking journalist who exposed Standard Oil)

assoc.t: Hurricane Ida, which struck Louisiana in 2021
Mount Ida, sacred mountain of Greek mythology

e.etymology: A modern name with no single source, close in sound to Kaya, Kaia and Kyla. It rose after 2018 with Kya Clark, heroine of the novel and film Where the Crawdads Sing.
namesakes: Kya Clark (heroine of Where the Crawdads Sing)
e.note: In Hindi and Urdu, kya is the everyday word for what.

assoc.t: Kya, the Marsh Girl of Where the Crawdads Sing

e.etymology: From the Arabic word amal (hope, aspiration), used for both girls and boys. A separate Indian boys' name Amal comes from Sanskrit amala (spotless, pure).
namesakes: Amal Clooney (human rights lawyer)

e.meaning: little Julia; traditionally read as youthful
e.etymology: A Latinate form of Juliet, which comes from Italian Giulietta, a pet form of Giulia (Julia). Julia is the feminine of the Roman family name Julius.
